section.title: Paul's Prayer of Thanksgiving
section.sectionRationale: Having poured out praise for the blessings of salvation, Paul now turns that praise into prayer. He does not ask for easier circumstances but for open eyes: that the Ephesians would truly know God and grasp the hope, the inheritance, and the power that are already theirs. That prayer then swells into a fresh vision of the risen and enthroned Christ, seated far above every power and given as head over all things for the church, His body.
section.thesis: Paul thanks God for the Ephesians' faith and love and prays that God would open the eyes of their hearts to know Him, the hope of His calling, the riches of their inheritance, and the surpassing power that raised Christ from the dead and enthroned Him above every power as head over all things for the church, His body.
section.frameNote: Three movements: thanksgiving for their faith and love; the prayer to know Him more, His hope, inheritance, and power; and the great vision of the power that raised and enthroned Christ as head over all for the church.

units.label: Thanksgiving for their faith and love
units.note: Paul does not stop giving thanks

verses.text: For this reason, ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints,
I have not stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, may give you a spirit of wisdom and {{apokalypsis|revelation}} in your {{epignosis|knowledge}} of Him.
I ask that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened, so that you may know the {{elpis|hope}} of His calling, the riches of His glorious {{kleronomia|inheritance}} in the saints,
and the surpassing greatness of His {{dynamis|power}} to us who believe. These are in accordance with the working of His mighty strength,

units.label: Christ raised and enthroned, head over all for the church

verses.text: which He exerted in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms,
far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the one to come.
And God put everything under His feet and made Him {{kephale|head}} over everything for the church,
which is His body, the {{pleroma|fullness}} of Him who fills all in all.

apokalypsis.gloss: Revelation, an unveiling or uncovering of what was hidden. Paul prays not merely for more information but for the Spirit to draw back the veil so the Ephesians truly perceive God. Such knowledge is a gift, given by the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, not achieved by human cleverness alone.

epignosis.gloss: Full or deep knowledge, a knowing that goes beyond bare acquaintance to real, personal recognition. The prefix strengthens the ordinary word for knowledge. Paul's aim is not that they learn about God at a distance but that they know Him truly and intimately, the very heart of what he asks for the church.

elpis.gloss: Hope, not a wishful maybe but a confident expectation grounded in God's promise. The hope of His calling is the certain future to which God has summoned His people. To know this hope is to live with assurance, seeing the destination God has fixed for those He has called.

kleronomia.gloss: Inheritance, the possession passed to an heir. Strikingly, Paul speaks of the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints, so that believers are God's own treasured inheritance. The word recalls Israel as the LORD's portion and now embraces the whole people God has redeemed as His prized possession.

dynamis.gloss: Power, might, the ability to accomplish. Paul heaps up words for power in verses 19 and 20 to describe the surpassing greatness of God's strength toward believers. It is no abstract force but the very same power that raised Christ from the dead, now at work in those who believe.

kephale.gloss: Head, carrying the sense of both authority over and source or origin. God made the risen Christ head over everything, and gave Him as head for the church, His body. Christ's headship means He rules all things and also supplies life and direction to His people, the body joined to Him.

pleroma.gloss: Fullness, completeness, the full measure. The church is called the fullness of Him who fills all in all, an astonishing phrase. It may mean that the church is that which Christ fills with His presence, or that the church completes Him as the body completes the head; either way it binds Christ and His people together in the closest union.

basic.context: After praising God for salvation, Paul turns to prayer. He thanks God constantly for the Ephesians' faith and love, and then he prays for the one thing they most need: to know God better. He asks that the eyes of their hearts would be opened to see the hope of God's calling, the riches of the inheritance, and the immeasurable power at work in them. That power, he says, is the very power that raised Jesus from the dead and seated Him above every ruler as head over all things for the church.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a prayer, and it teaches us what to pray for. Paul's deepest request is not for comfort or success but for spiritual sight, that believers would grasp what is already true of them in Christ. The prayer flows without a break into a description of Christ's resurrection and enthronement, so that the answer to the prayer is nothing less than a clearer vision of the exalted Lord and His finished work.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul asks God to give a spirit of wisdom and apokalypsis, revelation, an unveiling, in the epignosis, the deep personal knowledge, of God. He prays they would know the elpis, the confident hope, of God's calling, the riches of God's kleronomia, inheritance, in the saints, and the surpassing dynamis, power, toward those who believe. That power raised Christ and made Him kephale, head, over all things for the church, which is His pleroma, fullness.
basic.typology: Christ seated at God's right hand fulfills Psalm 110, where the LORD invites His anointed to sit at His right hand until His enemies are made a footstool. All things put under His feet fulfills Psalm 8, the dominion given to man, now realized in the risen Christ, the true and last Adam who reigns over all creation.
basic.christ: The prayer climaxes in a soaring portrait of Christ: raised from the dead, seated at God's right hand in the heavenly realms, exalted far above every rule, authority, power, and dominion, and above every name in this age and the next. God has put everything under His feet and given Him as head over all things for the church. The exalted Christ is the answer to the church's every need and fear.
basic.god: God is here the glorious Father, the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the source of wisdom and revelation and the one whose mighty strength raised and enthroned Jesus. He is the giver who delights to open blind eyes, and the sovereign who has placed all things under His Son's feet. The same God who wields resurrection power directs it toward those who believe.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 110 pictures the LORD's anointed seated at His right hand. Philippians 2 tells of the name above every name given to the exalted Christ. Colossians 1 names Christ the head of the body, the church, close kin to this passage.
basic.oneStory: The resurrection and enthronement of Christ are the turning point of the whole story. The power that made the world and will remake it has already been unleashed in raising Jesus and seating Him above every power. The church, His body, is joined to this reigning Lord, and the prayer that we would see it clearly is the prayer that we would live in the light of the victory already won.

context.literary:
Ephesians 1:15 to 23 is a thanksgiving that turns into a prayer, and the prayer turns into a creed. The Greek continues the long flow of chapter 1, so verses 15 to 23 are again a single, winding sentence. Paul begins with 'for this reason,' tying the prayer to the blessing before it: because God has done all that, he prays that they will see it. Verses 15 and 16 give the thanksgiving, verses 17 to 19 give the petition, and verses 20 to 23 explain the power behind it by rehearsing what God did to Christ.

The petition has a clear structure. One main request, that God would give 'a spirit of wisdom and revelation in your knowledge of Him,' verse 17, is unpacked by a second clause, 'the eyes of your heart may be enlightened,' verse 18, which in turn names three things to be known: the hope of His calling, the riches of His inheritance in the saints, and the greatness of His power toward us. The three objects look to the past, present and future in turn. Hope looks ahead, inheritance describes what God has in His people, and power describes what is at work now.

The word for power is stacked up in verse 19 with four different terms, which the English renders as 'power,' 'working,' 'mighty,' and 'strength.' Paul is straining to find words big enough. He then roots the whole thing in a historical event, the resurrection and enthronement of Christ, so that abstract power gets a face. The prayer ends in verses 22 and 23 by moving from Christ over all to Christ for the church, and the church is called His body. The movement is from the individual reader's eyes, to the universe's rulers, to the one body that will carry the news.
context.historical:
Paul prays for people he has heard about, which fits the circular character of the letter and the fact that he was writing from imprisonment. Their faith in the Lord Jesus and their love for 'all the saints' were known to him, and the second, love for the whole Christian family across lines of Jew and Gentile, was a notable thing in a world that sorted people by tribe and class.

The setting also explains the stress on power. In Ephesus the culture was full of spiritual forces, charms, amulets and astrology, and Acts 19:18 and 19 shows converts burning magic books worth a very large sum. People lived under a sense that unseen powers governed fate. Paul's list in verse 21, 'rule and authority, power and dominion,' uses the common vocabulary for such forces, whether he means angelic or demonic beings, human rulers, or both. To readers anxious about those forces, the claim that Christ sits far above every name was a direct word of comfort.

The picture of 'seated at His right hand' also had a very specific meaning. Seats at the right of a king were places of delegated authority, and the language comes from Psalm 110:1, a royal psalm that early Christians read as spoken to the Messiah. Peter had already said in Acts 2:33 to 36 that Jesus' exaltation fulfilled it. Paul's readers would have heard that the crucified Nazarene, whom Rome had executed, was in fact the one enthroned. A man executed by Roman power now outranks Roman power and every unseen power behind it.
context.canonical:
The prayer for knowledge has deep roots. Prayers for understanding and enlightenment appear in the Psalms, for example 'Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law,' Psalm 119:18. Isaiah 11:2 describes the Spirit of wisdom and understanding resting on the Messiah, and Paul asks that a share of that Spirit be given to believers. He prays similarly in Colossians 1:9 to 12 and Ephesians 3:14 to 19, where the request is for strength and a knowledge of Christ's love that surpasses knowledge.

The heart of verses 20 to 23 is made of two Old Testament texts. 'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet,' Psalm 110:1, supplies the seating and subjection. 'You have placed everything under his feet,' Psalm 8:6, supplies the 'put everything under His feet' of verse 22, a verse about the dignity given to humanity at creation. Paul reads Psalm 8 as finding its true fulfilment in the Son, as Hebrews 2:6 to 9 also does, and 1 Corinthians 15:25 to 28 says the same about Christ's reign until everything is under His feet.

The resurrection as the display of power runs through the New Testament. Romans 1:4 says Jesus was declared Son of God with power by the resurrection, and Romans 8:11 says the same Spirit who raised Him lives in believers. Philippians 2:9 to 11 and Colossians 2:9 and 10 and 1 Peter 3:22 repeat the theme of the exalted Christ and subject powers. The church as His body and the fullness of Christ is picked up in Ephesians 4:10 to 16, and in Colossians 1:18 and 24. The ultimate close is in Revelation 5 and 19, where the exalted Lamb is named King of kings.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul tells the Ephesians what he asks for them, and in doing so tells them what to want. He could have prayed for their safety or comfort in a hostile city. Instead, he prays that they would grasp three things, hope, inheritance and power, and he wants to be sure they overhear him praying it. A prayer that is written into a letter is also a lesson. By the time they reach verse 19, he wants them confident that the same might that raised Christ is at work in their own lives.

The target is also a shift in what they think is big. In a city dominated by great temples and unseen powers, Paul wants them to see that the real height is Christ's, and the real strength is the strength that raised Him. He also intends them to see the church differently. They are small and scattered, but verse 22 says Christ is head over everything 'for the church.' The church is the thing the universe's ruler cares about most. That is meant to give them dignity and to prepare them for what comes next in chapter 2, where Jew and Gentile are made into one body.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a record of an apostle's prayer, not a command to pray in these exact words, though it is clearly meant to be a model. We are free, and encouraged, to pray as Paul prays, asking for spiritual sight and not only circumstances. What the passage does not say is that anyone should expect a particular experience or a visible display of power in their own life as proof that they have what Paul asks. The power is described as 'toward us who believe,' and the evidence offered is the resurrection of Christ, not a pattern of felt experiences.

The second half, verses 20 to 23, is description of something already done: Christ was raised, seated, and given headship. Believers do not carry it out; they trust it and live from it. The application is therefore to pray for understanding, to rest on what is already true, and to take a place within the body of the one who rules, serving others in it, not to try to take charge of unseen powers by technique.

debates.question: Is the 'spirit of wisdom and revelation' the Holy Spirit or a human disposition?

views.label: The Holy Spirit, who gives wisdom and revelation
views.case: Paul has just spoken of the Spirit in verses 13 and 14, and in the Old Testament the Spirit rests on the Messiah as 'the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,' Isaiah 11:2. Revelation and knowledge of God come through the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 2:10 to 12, so Paul prays that the Spirit would give what only He can give.

views.label: A human spirit disposed to understand
views.case: The Greek word is not marked with the article and can be read as a spirit in the sense of an attitude or capacity, a wise and teachable heart, matching 'the eyes of your heart.' The believers already have the Holy Spirit, since they were sealed with Him, so the request is for a sharper receptivity.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not far apart, since a teachable heart is itself the Spirit's work. Either way the prayer asks that what is true would become seen and known, and the Giver is God.

debates.question: Does 'head' mean authority or source, and who fills whom in verse 23?

views.label: Head means rule, and Christ fills the church as He fills all things
views.case: The context is Psalm 110 and Psalm 8, which are about subjection and rule, and the head is placed over 'everything.' The phrase 'the fullness of Him who fills all in all' is read as Christ filling the church with His presence, which is how Ephesians 3:19 and 4:10 speak.

views.label: The church completes Christ
views.case: 'Fullness' is read as that which fills up or completes, so the church is the fullness of Christ as a body is the fullness of its head, meaning that the church is the place where He is manifested to the world. Ephesians 4:13 speaks of the church reaching 'the fullness of Christ.'

views.label: Head means source as well as authority
views.case: Some point to Ephesians 4:15 and 16, where the body grows from the head, and Colossians 2:19. The language of nourishment and growth suggests Christ is the source of the church's life as well as its ruler.

debates.bearing: The immediate setting makes rule the clear emphasis, and the closing phrase is best read as describing the exalted Lord who fills everything. Nothing in the text allows the church to be viewed as adding to Christ's sufficiency; the church is filled and not the filler.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the words the basic study names, several constructions in this passage carry a great deal.

The first is the tense of 'enlightened.' In verse 18 the phrase 'the eyes of your heart may be enlightened' is built on a perfect participle, which in Greek describes a completed action with a lasting result. The sense is 'having been enlightened,' so that the eyes of the heart are lit and stay lit. The heart is the Hebrew idea of the centre of mind, will and desire, not only emotion, so Paul's picture is of the whole inner person seeing.

Second, the word for 'calling' in verse 18 is built on the verb to call and, in Paul, refers to God's effective summons that brings people to Himself, not to an invitation that may be ignored. Paul can say in Romans 8:30 that those whom He called, He justified. The 'hope of His calling' is the hope that call carries with it.

Third, verse 19 pours out four words for power. The 'surpassing greatness' uses a compound built on the idea of throwing beyond, a word for what exceeds every measure, and Paul uses cognates of it in 2 Corinthians 4:7 and Ephesians 2:7 and 3:19. Then comes dynamis, 'power,' which is the lexicon word, energeia, 'working,' the root of our word energy and used for active, effective operation, kratos, 'strength,' which suggests might that rules, and ischys, 'might,' meaning inherent force. Paul stacks these because no single word is enough. He then uses a verb from the same root as energeia in verse 20, 'which He exerted,' showing that the power was not a stored potential but an action performed.

Fourth, verse 20 names two actions by past tense verbs, 'raised' and 'seated.' The verb for 'seated' is the ordinary word for sitting down in a place of rule, and verse 22 follows with 'put everything under His feet,' which uses a compound of 'to arrange under,' quoting the Greek of Psalm 8:6. The four terms in verse 21, rule, authority, power and dominion, are a list of ranks, in the Greek, archē, exousia, dynamis and kyriotes. Paul uses lists like this in Colossians 1:16 and Ephesians 6:12. They are intentionally comprehensive, not a precise chart of angelic orders.

Finally, the last phrase, 'who fills all in all,' uses a participle that can be read as either middle or passive. If middle, Christ fills all things for Himself; if passive, He is being filled. Most translations take it as a statement that He fills everything. The ambiguity is part of why the verse is debated, and the translation difficulty is worth noting for anyone building doctrine on it.

typology.type: The royal enthronement of David's son
typology.fulfillment: Psalm 110:1 gave a king seated at the LORD's right hand while enemies became a footstool, language rooted in the kings of David's line and the promise of 2 Samuel 7:12 and 13. Paul says the promised Son sits there now. The pattern of Israel's anointed king, who ruled for a while and died, is surpassed by a king raised from death who 'always lives,' Hebrews 7:25. The type falls short in every earthly king, who ruled only a small place for a short time, while this King holds 'every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the one to come.'

Psalm 8:6 says God put everything under man's feet, a restatement of Genesis 1:26 to 28. Hebrews 2:8 admits that 'at present we do not see everything subject to him.' Paul says the promise is kept in Christ, the true man, over whom nothing stands. The first Adam was given rule and lost it to the serpent, and the last Adam, raised and seated, takes it back, 1 Corinthians 15:27. The type is not yet complete in its visible form, since 1 Corinthians 15:25 says He must reign until all enemies are under His feet.

The picture of a people with a head runs through Israel's story, where leaders such as Moses and David stood at the head of the people. Paul takes the human body as a pattern and says the church is Christ's body. The pattern is stronger than a metaphor, because believers are joined to Him by the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 12:12 and 13. The type falls short because no human leader could give life to his people, whereas Christ nourishes the body from Himself, Ephesians 4:16.

When the tabernacle was finished the cloud covered it and the glory of the LORD filled it, Exodus 40:34, and the same happened at the temple, 1 Kings 8:10 and 11. Paul's talk of fullness in Christ and of the church as His fullness draws on this idea of a place filled with God's presence. Colossians 2:9 says all the fullness of the Deity lives in Christ in bodily form, and Ephesians 2:21 and 22 calls the church a holy temple. The tent and the temple could be left or destroyed, but Christ's body is a living house that cannot be dismantled.

study.christ:
Everything in this passage is about the person and work of Christ, and the angles are worth separating.

First, He is the Lord of the one praying. Paul speaks of 'the Lord Jesus' and the God of 'our Lord Jesus Christ' and in the next breath speaks of Christ seated at God's right hand. Jesus is placed in a position that in Jewish thinking belonged to God alone. Psalm 110:1 has two persons, the LORD and 'my Lord,' and Peter says in Acts 2:34 to 36 that the second is Jesus.

Second, He is the one raised. 'He exerted in Christ when He raised Him from the dead' is a statement that the resurrection was an act of the Father's power, and it is the centre of the Christian message. Romans 1:4 declares Jesus Son of God with power by the resurrection, and Romans 6:4 says Christ was raised 'through the glory of the Father.' The resurrection proves the cross worked, since death could not hold Him.

Third, He is the one enthroned. The Ascension is not a minor sequel. Hebrews 1:3 says that after providing purification for sins He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and Philippians 2:9 says God exalted Him to the highest place. The Christ who was humiliated is now the highest. Matthew 28:18 gives His own claim: 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.'

Fourth, He is the head. The title does not only say He rules. It says He relates to the church as a head to a body, so that the church is not a separate organisation that He supervises but a living unit joined to Him. Colossians 1:18 says He is 'the head of the body, the church.' The church receives life, direction and growth from Him, Ephesians 4:15 and 16.

Fifth, He is the fullness. All the fullness of God dwells in Him, Colossians 1:19, and He fills all in all. John 1:16 says 'from His fullness we have all received grace upon grace.' The church, as His body, is the place where His fullness is displayed and communicated.

Sixth, He is the one in whom we are included. Ephesians 2:6 says that God raised believers up with Christ and seated them with Him, so the same movement of death, resurrection and enthronement, which is His, is also ours. Colossians 3:1 to 4 says believers are raised with Christ and their life is hidden with Him in God.

A caution against forcing the text. The 'footstool' is a picture of conquest and does not need to be spiritualised into something else, and the 'feet' of the body need not be assigned to particular groups. The links to Christ are given by Paul, and the passage is rich enough without adding more.
study.god:
This prayer reveals God as the glorious Father, the giver of wisdom, and the one whose power raised the dead. Several features of the doctrine of God are visible.

First, He is the 'glorious Father' and 'the God of our Lord Jesus Christ,' verse 17. Both phrases appear together, and they show that the Father is God to the Son in His human obedience and Father in His eternal relation. The one God has made Himself known as the Father of the Lord Jesus. This is why Paul can pray to Him with such confidence, since the God addressed is the one who has already shown what He can do.

Second, He is a God who gives knowledge of Himself. Paul asks God to give a spirit of wisdom and revelation. Knowledge of God is not something that humans reach by their own effort. He discloses Himself. 1 Corinthians 2:9 to 12 says the Spirit searches the deep things of God and reveals them. In the doctrine of God, this means God is not merely an object of study but a person who chooses to be known.

Third, He is a God of power, and the passage insists that this power is shown in a specific event, not in the abstract. The power that raised Christ is the standard by which we measure what God can do for us. Isaiah 40:26 speaks of the One who made the stars 'because of His great power and mighty strength,' and Paul uses the same pairing of power and strength. The doctrine is not that God can do anything in a vague sense, but that He has done this, and so there is no situation His people face in which the raising of the dead is not the measure.

Fourth, He is a God who rules through His Son. The Father seats the Son and puts everything under His feet. The persons are distinct, the Father acting and the Son receiving, and yet the rule is one. 1 Corinthians 15:24 to 28 says the Son will hand the kingdom to the Father so that God may be all in all, so the Son's reign is also a reign in service of the Father's glory. The Father is not diminished by the Son's exaltation; it is His work.

Fifth, He is a God with a purpose for the church. Christ is head over all things 'for the church.' God has chosen to work through a body of people. Ephesians 3:10 says that through the church the manifold wisdom of God is made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms.

For worship this passage invites two responses. One is thanks, as Paul begins with thanksgiving. The other is awe at power that is not frightening because it is on our side. A God whose strength is that great is also a God whose love, by the same text, is directed toward 'us who believe.'

crossReferences.note: 'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' This is the source of verses 20 and 22. Paul reads the royal psalm as fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and ascension, with the footstool as the subjection of every power.

'You have placed everything under his feet.' Paul quotes the line about humanity's rule over creation and applies it to Christ, the true man who holds the rule Adam was given and lost. Hebrews 2:6 to 9 makes the same move.

A second prayer in the same letter, this time for strength through the Spirit, Christ dwelling in hearts by faith, and knowing a love that surpasses knowledge. It shows what the 'knowledge of Him' in 1:17 looks like when it grows.

Christ as image of the invisible God, creator of thrones and dominions, head of the body, the firstborn from the dead. It supplies the background for 'every name that is named' and 'head over everything for the church.'

God exalted Christ to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names, so that every knee should bow. It is the same enthronement from another angle, and shows the exaltation follows the cross.
The Spirit of Him who raised Jesus lives in believers and will give life to mortal bodies. It carries the resurrection power of verse 20 into the believer's own experience and future.

Christ reigns until all enemies are under His feet, with death the last, and then hands the kingdom to the Father so that God may be all in all. It shows the end of the subjection that Ephesians 1:22 describes as already established in principle.
Christ is the head from whom the whole body grows and builds itself up in love. It fills out 'head over everything for the church' with the picture of nourishment and growth.

In Christ the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form, and believers 'have been made complete in Christ, who is the head over every ruler and authority.' It supports the fullness language of verse 23 and the same triumph over rulers.
The Spirit of the LORD rests on the Messiah as 'the Spirit of wisdom and understanding.' It stands behind Paul's request for a spirit of wisdom and revelation, now asked for the Messiah's people.

study.oneStory:
This prayer stands where the Bible's story of rule and rescue is told at its fullest. In Genesis 1:26 to 28 humanity is given rule over the world, and Psalm 8 sings of it. In Genesis 3 that rule is surrendered, and the world falls under powers that humans were meant to govern. The story from there is the search for the true man who will rule rightly. Israel's kings, from David on, were shadows of the one who would sit at the right hand of God and have all things placed under His feet. Ephesians 1:20 to 23 is the announcement that the one has come, died, been raised and seated.

What does this answer from before? The question of why a good world is full of hostile powers and why God has not simply ended them. The answer is that God has begun the reversal by raising His Son and putting Him over those powers, though not yet all in visible form, as Hebrews 2:8 admits. It also answers the longing of the Psalms and Prophets for a king whose rule would bring peace, and the long Old Testament cry for God to act in power as He did at the exodus. The exodus was the great act of power in the Old Testament, and the resurrection is the greater.

What does it set up? Chapter 2, immediately, where Paul says that the power which raised Christ also raised those who were dead in sin and seated them with Him. Then the unity of Jew and Gentile in one body, the church, which is the first sign in history of the gathered universe promised in verse 10 of the first chapter. After that, the call to live as people who share Christ's victory, and the warning in 6:12 that the struggle with the powers is not over, so that believers must stand in the strength of the Lord, 6:10.

How does it end? In 1 Corinthians 15:24 to 28 the last enemy is destroyed and the Son hands over the kingdom so that God is all in all. Revelation 5:9 to 13 and 11:15 show the whole creation worshipping, and Revelation 21 to 22 show the place where God dwells with His people and the Lamb's throne is in the city. The prayer of Paul is that the Ephesians would see now, with the eyes of the heart, what the whole world will see then.

quiz.q: What does Paul chiefly pray for the Ephesians?

options.text: That God would open the eyes of their hearts to know Him more deeply.
options.note: His central request is for spiritual sight and knowledge of God.

options.text: That God would remove all their hardships and troubles.
options.note: A natural wish, but Paul prays for insight, not easier circumstances.

options.text: That they would gain wealth and social standing.
options.note: The riches he names are spiritual, the inheritance and power of God.

options.text: That they would earn God's favor by their efforts.
options.note: The blessings are already theirs; he prays they would see them.

quiz.q: What are the three things Paul wants them to know in verses 18 and 19?

options.text: The hope of His calling, the riches of His inheritance, and His surpassing power.
options.note: These are the three objects of the enlightened heart's knowledge.

options.text: Their giftedness, their reputation, and their comfort.
options.note: The passage names hope, inheritance, and power, not personal status.

options.text: The hope of heaven only, with nothing for the present.
options.note: Hope is one part, but Paul also names the inheritance and present power.

options.text: The rules they must keep to stay saved.
options.note: Paul prays for insight into grace, not a list of requirements.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the power at work toward believers?

options.text: It is the same power that raised Christ and seated Him at God's right hand.
options.note: Verses 19 and 20 define the power by the resurrection and enthronement.

options.text: It is a vague, impersonal force in the universe.
options.note: It is God's own mighty strength, shown in raising Jesus.

options.text: It is a power only some elite believers can access.
options.note: Paul says it is toward us who believe, all who trust Christ.

options.text: It is a power that has not yet begun to work.
options.note: It has already worked mightily in raising Christ from the dead.

quiz.q: Where is the risen Christ seated, and over what?

options.text: At God's right hand, far above every rule, authority, power, and dominion.
options.note: Verses 20 and 21 place Him above every power and name.

options.text: Among the ranks of the angels as one power among many.
options.note: He is far above all such powers, not one among them.

options.text: In authority over this present age but not the age to come.
options.note: He reigns above every name in this age and the one to come.

options.text: In a waiting place until He earns His throne.
options.note: He is already enthroned with everything under His feet.

quiz.q: What relationship does the passage draw between Christ and the church?

options.text: He is head over all things for the church, which is His body.
options.note: Verses 22 and 23 name Christ the head and the church His body.

options.text: The church rules over Christ as its servant.
options.note: Christ is the head; the church is His body under Him.

options.text: The church is unrelated to Christ's cosmic reign.
options.note: His reign over all things is precisely for the church.

options.text: The church is only loosely connected to Christ.
options.note: The union is intimate: body to head, filled with His fullness.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the church is His fullness?

options.text: The church is bound to Christ in closest union as the body filled with His presence.
options.note: Fullness binds Christ and His people in intimate union.

options.text: The church supplies something Christ truly lacked.
options.note: Christ needs nothing; He graciously chooses to fill and join His body.

options.text: The church replaces Christ as the source of life.
options.note: Christ remains the head; the church is filled by Him, not a substitute.

options.text: The phrase has no real meaning for believers.
options.note: It gives the church astonishing dignity as the place His fullness dwells.

questions: Paul's deepest prayer for his friends is that they would know God better. When you pray for people you love, how often do you ask for their spiritual sight rather than only their circumstances?
Paul asks that the eyes of your heart be enlightened. Where do you need God to open your eyes to a hope, an inheritance, or a power that is already yours in Christ?
The same power that raised Jesus from the dead is at work toward you. How would facing this week change if you really believed resurrection power was available to you?
Christ is seated far above every rule and authority and every name that is named. What powers or fears in your life need to be seen in the light of His reign over them all?
You belong to the body of the Christ who fills all in all. How does being joined to the reigning Lord shape the way you see the church and your place in it?

translationNotes.note: A spirit of wisdom and revelation may refer to the Holy Spirit who gives these gifts or to a disposition He works; either way the wisdom and revelation are God's gift, not human achievement.
His glorious inheritance in the saints most likely means God's own inheritance, that is, His people as His treasured possession, though some read it as the inheritance God gives to the saints.
The fullness of Him who fills all in all can be read actively, the church as that which Christ fills, or as the church completing Him as body to head; the Greek allows both and stresses their union.
